autor: Laurence of Březová (c. 1370–after 1437), master of the Prague university
quelle: Vavřinec z Březové, Kronika husitská, ed. J. Goll, Fontes rerum Bohemicarum V (Prague 1893), pp. 344–396. Page images: Czech Academy of Sciences, FONTES, book 1103; machine text: AHISTO portal, Masaryk University. Public domain.
hinweis: Goll prints Laurence's Latin beside an old Czech translation; only the Latin is carried, read against the page images. Excerpts from July 1419 to July 1420; cuts are marked [...]. The companion site The Hussite Field Armies carries the chronicle from 22 August 1420 on. The English is this site's working translation (CC0).

sections.titel: 1419: Tábor, the town hall, the king's death
sections.blurb: The summer the movement became a revolt: forty thousand at communion on a mountain they called Tábor, the New Town councillors thrown from the town hall by the people and Jan Žižka, and King Wenceslas dead within three weeks.

units.orig: Item anno domini MCCCCXIX sacerdotes evangelici Magistro Johanni Hus faventes et communionem calicis ad populum communem promoventes, tunc Wikleffiste et alias Hussite nuncupati, cum populo sexus utriusque ex diversis regni Bohemie partibus, civitatibus et villis cum sacramento eukaristie in montem quendam prope castrum Bechina, quem montem Thabor appellaverunt, frequentare ceperunt et ibidem populum communem sacra eukaristia precipue diebus festivis magna cum reverencia communicabant, emulis ipsius communionis populum communem in ecclesiis adiacentibus sic communicare non permittentibus. In festo autem sancte Marie Magdalene magna multitudine populi sexus utriusque et eciam parvulorum ad prefatum montem congregata de diversis regni prefati partibus, ultra quam XL millia personarum sacramento corporis et sanguinis domini sub utraque specie, panis scilicet et vini, secundum tradicionem Christi et praxim ac observanciam primitive ecclesie magna communicaverunt cum devocione. Quam ob rem rex Bohemie Wenceslaus multum est turbatus, se de regali solio deici timens et expavescens, Nicolaumque de Hus in locum sui substitui suspicando [...].
units.en: Item, in the year of the Lord 1419, the evangelical priests who favoured Master Jan Hus and promoted the communion of the chalice for the common people, then called Wycliffites or Hussites, began to resort, with people of both sexes from various parts, towns and villages of the kingdom of Bohemia, with the sacrament of the Eucharist, to a certain mountain near the castle of Bechyně, which they called Mount Tábor; and there they gave the common people communion in the holy Eucharist with great reverence, especially on feast days, since the opponents of that communion would not allow the common people to communicate so in the neighbouring churches. And on the feast of St Mary Magdalene a great multitude of people of both sexes, and of children too, gathered at the said mountain from various parts of the kingdom, more than forty thousand persons, and received the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord in both kinds, bread and wine, according to the tradition of Christ and the practice and observance of the early Church, with great devotion. Because of this King Wenceslas of Bohemia was much disturbed, fearing and dreading that he would be cast down from the royal throne, and suspecting that Nicholas of Hus would be put in his place [...].
units.note: St Mary Magdalene's day is 22 July 1419. The name of the mountain is biblical: Tabor, the mount of the Transfiguration. Nicholas of Hus, a lord of southern Bohemia who had spoken for the chalice before the king, had been banished from Prague. The cut tells how. Laurence was a master of the Prague university and a moderate Utraquist, of the chalice but no friend of Tábor.

units.titel: The councillors thrown from the town hall
units.orig: Item anno eodem dominico die post Jacobi, alias XXX die mensis Julii, magister civium et consules aliqui Nove civitatis cum subiudice, communionis calicis emuli, per communem populum et Johannem Ziskam, regis Bohemie prefati familiarem, pro eo quod processioni illic iuxta pretorium cum sacramento venerabili eukaristie a sancto Stephano in Rybniczka ad monasterium beate Virginis in Arena redeunti insultaverunt, sunt de pretorio Nove civitatis enormiter deiecti et atrociter mactati et interfecti, rege Wenceslao pro tunc in Novo castro unum fere milliare a Praga distante cum sua curia consistente. Propter quod opus emulos veritatis in Praga magnus timor invasit [...]. Communitas vero ipsa quatuor capitaneos sibi usque ad futurorum eleccionem scabinorum elegit, quibus sigillum et alia consulatus insignia assignavit [...]. Unde rex Bohemie Wenceslaus ira magna motus et angustia ac dolore perturbatus proposuit omnes Wikleffistas seu Hussitas, et precipue sacerdotes extirpare. [...] Finaliter ergo parte utraque consenciente concluditur, quatenus communitas Nove civitatis se ipsi regi pro excessu, quem in deiciendo scabinos ab ipso deputatos et turpiter mactatos commiserat, humiliet et rex novos scabinos per ipsam tunc communitatem electos confirmet, quod et factum est cum effectu.
units.en: Item, in the same year, on the Sunday after St James, that is the 30th day of July, the burgomaster and some councillors of the New Town with the under-judge, opponents of the communion of the chalice, were outrageously thrown down from the town hall of the New Town by the common people and by Jan Žižka, a familiar of the said king of Bohemia, and were cruelly butchered and killed, because they had insulted a procession with the venerable sacrament of the Eucharist returning past the town hall from St Stephen's in Rybníček to the monastery of the Blessed Virgin in Na Písku; King Wenceslas was at that time at Nový Hrad, about a mile from Prague, with his court. Because of this deed a great fear fell on the opponents of the truth in Prague [...]. The community itself chose four captains until new aldermen should be elected, and handed over to them the seal and the other insignia of the council [...]. At this King Wenceslas of Bohemia, moved with great anger and troubled with anguish and grief, resolved to root out all the Wycliffites or Hussites, and above all the priests. [...] At last, with the consent of both sides, it was agreed that the community of the New Town should humble itself before the king for the excess it had committed in throwing down and shamefully killing the aldermen he had appointed, and that the king should confirm the new aldermen whom the community had then elected; and this was done in fact.
units.note: The first defenestration of Prague, 30 July 1419. Laurence names two agents, 'the common people' and Jan Žižka, here still 'a familiar of the king', a minor courtier; it is Žižka's first appearance in the chronicle. Modern accounts add that the procession was led by the preacher Jan Želivský; Laurence does not name him here. The town council had been appointed by the king; the deed was rebellion against him, and the settlement, the town humbled and its new aldermen confirmed, was the king's last act of authority in Prague. The cuts describe the summons to arms, the flight of the opponents and the negotiations.

units.orig: Item anno eodem feria IV post Assumpcionem beate virginis Marie, que erat dies XVI mensis Augusti, rex Bohemie Wenceslaus hora quasi vesperorum apoplexia percussus cum magno clamore et rugitu quasi leonis subito est extinctus in Novo castro prope Pragam, cuius corpus post dies aliquot propter timorem populi tempore nocturno ad castrum Pragense est deductum et in capella sancti Wenceslai, Boemorum patroni, collocatum et post septimanas aliquot abinde ad monasterium Aule Regie, ubi sepulturam sibi eligerat, noctis tempore miserrime transductum et a piscatoribus, pistoribus et conversis monasterii eiusdem sepultum. Cuius mors et acta ipsius cunctis regibus deberent fore in exemplum, quatenus deum timeant et eius legem ac veritatem pro posse tueantur et defendant.
units.en: Item, in the same year, on the Wednesday after the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which was the 16th day of August, Wenceslas, king of Bohemia, struck by apoplexy at about the hour of vespers, died suddenly with a great cry and a roar like a lion's at Nový Hrad near Prague. After some days his body was carried by night, for fear of the people, to Prague Castle and laid in the chapel of St Wenceslas, patron of the Bohemians; and some weeks later it was taken from there by night, most wretchedly, to the monastery of Aula Regia, where he had chosen his burial, and buried by the fishermen, bakers and lay brothers of that monastery. His death and his deeds ought to be an example to all kings, that they may fear God and protect and defend his law and truth as far as they can.
units.note: Wenceslas IV died eighteen days after the defenestration. Aula Regia is the Cistercian abbey of Zbraslav south of Prague. The heir was his half-brother Sigismund, king of Hungary and of the Romans, who had given Hus his safe conduct. Laurence's moral is pointed: a king should defend God's law, and Wenceslas, as the chronicler saw it, had not.

sections.titel: The crusade before Prague and the battle of Vítkov
sections.blurb: All Christendom before one city, 'Hus! Hus! Heretic!' shouted from the hill, Žižka's log fort on Vítkov, and the battle of 14 July 1420 won with stones, flails and the sacrament.

units.orig: In hoc ergo exercitu, cuius multitudo ultra quam ad centum quinquaginta millia armatorum se extendebant, erant enim archiepiscopi, episcopi, patriarcha Aquilegiensis, doctores diversi ceterique prelati spirituales, duces et principes seculares, numero fere XL, marchiones, comites, barones et nobiles multi, milites, clientes, cives diversarum civitatum et rustici totam planiciem camporum premissorum occupando et tentoria seu tabernacula sumptuosa in similitudinem trium magnarum civitatum ordinando. Ibi diversarum nacionum fuere populi, tribus et lingue, Boemi et Moravi, Hungari et Croaci, Dalmaci et Bulgari, Walachi et Siculi, Cuni, Jasi, Ruteni, Rasi, Slavi, Pruteni, Servi, Turingi, Stirii, Misnenses, Bavari, Saxones, Australes, Franci, Francones, Anglici, Brabanti, Bestfali, Holandri, Sweyceri, Lusacenses, Swevi, Carintii, Aragones, Hispani, Poloni, Theutonici de Reno et alii quam plurimi. Hii ergo cottidie in vertice montis supra flumen ex opposito monasterii sancte Crucis et ecclesie sancti Valentini stantes contra civitatem ha! ha! hus! hus! kacer! kacer! velut canes ululabant [...].
units.en: In this army, whose numbers ran to more than a hundred and fifty thousand armed men, there were archbishops, bishops, the patriarch of Aquileia, various doctors and other spiritual prelates, secular dukes and princes to the number of about forty, margraves, counts, barons and many nobles, knights, squires, citizens of various towns and peasants, occupying the whole plain of the said fields and setting out costly tents and pavilions like three great cities. There were peoples, tribes and tongues of various nations: Bohemians and Moravians, Hungarians and Croats, Dalmatians and Bulgarians, Wallachians and Szeklers, Cumans, Jassians, Ruthenians, Rascians, Slavs, Prussians, Serbs, Thuringians, Styrians, Meisseners, Bavarians, Saxons, Austrians, French, Franconians, English, Brabanters, Westphalians, Hollanders, Swiss, Lusatians, Swabians, Carinthians, Aragonese, Spaniards, Poles, Germans from the Rhine and very many others. These stood every day on the top of the hill above the river opposite the monastery of the Holy Cross and the church of St Valentine, and howled at the city like dogs: 'Ha! ha! Hus! Hus! Kacer! Kacer!' [...]
units.note: The crusade proclaimed by Pope Martin V on 1 March 1420 against the heretics of Bohemia, under the command of Sigismund, before Prague in June and July 1420. Laurence's numbers are the chronicler's; modern estimates are much lower. 'Kacer' is the German Ketzer, heretic. The list of nations is the point: all Christendom against one city. The cut says that Bohemians who fell into the crusaders' hands were burned as heretics even if they had never taken the chalice.

units.orig: Item cum rex Hungarie Sigismundus sic potenter, ut prefertur, campos cum intraneis et extraneis contra Pragensem teneret civitatem et intenderet montem prope patibulum dictum Witkowa hora suis munire gentibus, ut velut tercio castro Pragam sic stringeret, quod nullus civitati Pragensi liber pateret victualium accessus, hoc presciens Johannes Ziska, Thaboriensium capitaneus, absque dilacione mox in supradicto monte duo in modum stubarum disposuit fieri propugnacula, que parvulo fossato circumfodi mandavit et muro ex humo et lapidibus circumdari, per quod quidem propugnaculum dominus omnipotens miraculose salutem Pragensi contulit civitati, ita quod in eodem loco hostes prostrati amplius civitatem sic hostiliter invadere non attemptaverunt, ut patebit inferius.
units.en: Item, when Sigismund, king of Hungary, held the fields so powerfully against the city of Prague, as said above, with natives and foreigners, and intended to occupy with his men the hill near the gallows called Vítkova hora, so as to squeeze Prague as with a third castle, so that no free access for victuals should be open to the city of Prague, Jan Žižka, captain of the Taborites, knowing this beforehand, at once had two strongpoints built on that hill in the manner of log houses, which he ordered to be ringed with a small ditch and surrounded with a wall of earth and stones; and by this strongpoint Almighty God miraculously gave salvation to the city of Prague, so that the enemy, defeated in that place, did not again attempt to attack the city in this way, as will appear below.
units.note: A year after the defenestration the king's familiar is 'captain of the Taborites'. The crusaders held Prague Castle and Vyšehrad; Vítkov, the long hill east of the Old Town, would have been the third grip on the city, closing the road by which supplies came in.

units.titel: The battle on the hill, 14 July 1420
units.orig: Item in crastino, scilicet die dominico post Margarethe proximo, quasi hora vesperorum aptus fuit omnis regis exercitus, ut quidam ex eis in pluribus millibus ligneum in monte iuxta patibulum per Ziskam erectum propugnaculum expugnando invaderent, quo habito cetere turme secundum capitaneorum disposicionem in Pragensem in tribus locis irruerent civitatem [...]. Misnenses vero cum suis et sibi VII vel VIII millibus iunctis equestres montem ascendunt et cum impetu et tubicenis pretactum ligneum invadunt propugnaculum fossatam et turrim vinee obtinentes. Et cum murum ex terra et lapidibus factum vellent ascendere, due mulieres cum una virgine et forte cum XXVI viris, qui pro tunc in propugnaculo remanserant, viriliter lapidibus et cuspidibus resistentes defendebant, telis enim et pixidum pulvere carentes. Una itaque ex pretactis mulieribus, licet inermis, virorum vincebat animum nolens a loco suo pedem retrahere: „Antichristo, inquit, non licet fideli christiano cedere.“ Et sic animose pugnans interfecta spiritum exalavit. Ziska quoque veniens et ipse prostratus fuisset, nisi sui cum trituris eum de hostium manibus eruissent. Et cum iam tota quasi civitas de perdicione formidaret, oraciones et lacrimas cum parvulis fundens solum auxilium de celo prestolabatur, advenit interim presbiter cum corporis Christi sacramento et post eum quinquaginta forte sagittarii et ceteri rustici inermes cum trituris et inimici viso sacramento et audito campanule sono magnoque populi clamore vehementi timore prostrati terga vertunt cicius fugientes, alter alterum cupiens in cursu prevenire. [...] Quo facto rex cum omni exercitu silenter ad tentoria rediit ira, tedio, planctu et dolore repletus. Pragenses vero flexis in campo Hospitalensi genibus grates deo persolvunt Te deum laudamus altis vocibus personantes, quia non robore eorum, sed miraculose in paucis eis de hostibus dedit victoriam.
units.en: Item, on the next day, that is the Sunday after St Margaret, at about the hour of vespers, the whole of the king's army was ready: some thousands of them were to storm the wooden strongpoint built by Žižka on the hill by the gallows, and when it was taken the other troops, as the captains had arranged, were to fall on the city of Prague in three places [...]. The Meisseners with their men, and seven or eight thousand horsemen joined to them, climbed the hill and with a rush and trumpets attacked the said wooden strongpoint, taking the ditch and the tower of the vineyard. And when they tried to climb the wall made of earth and stones, two women with a girl and perhaps twenty-six men, who had stayed in the strongpoint at that moment, defended it manfully, resisting with stones and spears, for they had no arrows and no powder for their guns. One of these women, though unarmed, surpassed the courage of men, refusing to draw her foot back from her place: 'A faithful Christian,' she said, 'must not yield to Antichrist.' And so, fighting bravely, she was killed and breathed out her spirit. Žižka too, coming up, would himself have been struck down if his men had not rescued him from the enemy's hands with their flails. And when the whole city was already in fear of its ruin, pouring out prayers and tears with its children and waiting only for help from heaven, there came a priest with the sacrament of the body of Christ, and after him perhaps fifty archers and other unarmed peasants with flails; and the enemy, seeing the sacrament and hearing the sound of the little bell and the great shout of the people, were overcome with violent fear, turned their backs and fled, each wanting to outrun the other. [...] When this was done, the king returned silently with his whole army to the tents, full of anger, weariness, lamentation and grief. And the Praguers, kneeling in the field of the Hospital, gave thanks to God, singing the Te Deum with loud voices, because not by their strength but miraculously he had given them, few as they were, the victory over their enemies.
units.note: 14 July 1420. The Czech translation in the same edition reads sixteen men for Laurence's twenty-six. The flail, the peasant's threshing tool shod with iron, is the weapon of the day; the companion site follows it into Žižka's field armies. The cut tells of the crusaders falling from the steep rock in their flight, about three hundred killed within an hour. The next page says the hill was afterwards called Žižka's hill, after its founder, or the Hill of the Chalice; the district of Prague on its slope is still Žižkov.

sections.blurb: The programme sent to the crusading army in July 1420, in Latin, German and Czech: free preaching, the chalice, no worldly lordship for the clergy, and the punishment of public sins.

units.titel: 'By death or by life': the preamble, and the first article
units.orig: Item post predictam Theutonicorum factam inopinatam stragem quievit Praga civitas a frequenti hostium impulsu et non iam hus! hus! kacer! kacer! Theutonici proclamabant [...]. Ad que civitatis tractatores aiunt, se non posse sine consensu aliarum civitatum, cum quibus sunt ligati, aliquam inire concordiam, sed supplicant, quatenus propter ipsorum et regni tocius honorem apud regem publicam magistris et presbiteris obtineant audienciam, ut quatuor linguis, boemico, theutonico, hungarico et latino, valeant aperte veritates quatuor articulorum, pro quibus se Pragenses cum sibi adherentibus regi opponunt, lucide et aperte scripturis toti exercitui declarare [...]. Quapropter magistri Pragenses conscriptis IV articulis cum eorum probacionibus in latino, theutonico et boemico, ad exercitum direxerunt sub hac, que sequitur, forma: Nos magister civium, consules et scabini totaque communitas civitatis Pragensis capitalis regni Bohemie nostro et aliorum fidelium huiusmodi regni nomine instituimus etc. Notum sit universis Christi fidelibus, quod fideles in regno Boemie instant et domino iuvante instare proponunt sive per mortem, sive per vitam, quantum est eis possibile, pro articulis infrascriptis: Primo, quod verbum dei per regnum Bohemie libere et sine impedimento ordinate a sacerdotibus domini predicetur et nuncietur iuxta sentenciam salvatoris Marci ultimo: euntes in mundum universum predicate evangelium omni creature; et Mathie ultimo. Nam secundum apostolum verbum domini non est alligatum, sed orandum est secundum eundem, ut sermo dei currat et clarificetur ubique, ut dicitur IIa ad Thessal. III°. Et loqui linguis in ecclesia dei nemo debet prohiberi, ut dicitur prima ad Corinth. XIV°.
units.en: Item, after the unexpected slaughter of the Germans, the city of Prague rested from the frequent assaults of the enemy, and the Germans no longer shouted 'Hus! Hus! Kacer! Kacer!' [...] To which the city's negotiators said that they could make no agreement without the consent of the other towns with which they were bound, but they begged that, for their own honour and that of the whole kingdom, a public hearing before the king be obtained for the masters and priests, so that in four languages, Czech, German, Hungarian and Latin, they might set out plainly and clearly from the scriptures to the whole army the truths of the four articles for which the Praguers and those who adhered to them opposed the king [...]. Therefore the masters of Prague wrote down the four articles with their proofs in Latin, German and Czech and sent them to the army in the following form: We, the burgomaster, councillors and aldermen and the whole community of the city of Prague, capital of the kingdom of Bohemia, in our name and that of the other faithful of this kingdom, declare etc. Be it known to all the faithful of Christ that the faithful in the kingdom of Bohemia stand, and with the Lord's help intend to stand, by death or by life, as far as they are able, for the articles written below. First, that the word of God be preached and proclaimed freely and without hindrance, in good order, by the priests of the Lord throughout the kingdom of Bohemia, according to the saying of the Saviour in the last chapter of Mark: 'Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature'; and the last chapter of Matthew. For according to the apostle the word of God is not bound, but we must pray, as he says, that the word of God may run and be glorified everywhere (2 Thessalonians 3). And no one should be forbidden to speak in tongues in the church of God (1 Corinthians 14).
units.note: The Four Articles of Prague, the common programme of the Hussite parties, in the form sent to the crusading army in July 1420. The hearing was promised and never held: the cut tells how the barons on the king's side quarrelled over hostages until the talks lapsed. Free preaching is the first article because the conflict had begun with it: the ban of 1410 on preaching in chapels such as Hus's Bethlehem Chapel, which Hus defied.

units.orig: Secundo, quod sacramentum divinissime eukaristie sub utraque specie, scilicet panis et vini, omnibus Christi fidelibus nullo peccato mortali indispositis libere ministretur iuxta sentenciam et institucionem salvatoris, qui dixit: accipite et comedite, hoc est corpus meum, et bibite ex hoc omnes, hic est sanguis meus novi testamenti, qui pro multis effundetur Mathie XXVI°, Marci XIV°, Luce XXII°, ubi datur eciam preceptum apostolis, cum dicitur: hoc facite. [...]
units.en: Second, that the sacrament of the most divine Eucharist be given freely under both kinds, that is bread and wine, to all the faithful of Christ not disqualified by mortal sin, according to the word and institution of the Saviour, who said: 'Take and eat, this is my body; and drink of this, all of you, this is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many' (Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22), where a command is also given to the apostles in the words: 'Do this.' [...]
units.note: The chalice for the laity was not Hus's own cause: his friend Jakoubek of Stříbro began to give it in Prague in the autumn of 1414, while Hus was at Constance, and the council forbade it in June 1415. It became the sign of the movement, on banners, shields and church fronts. The cut is a page and a half of authorities, from the Gospel of John and Pope Gelasius to Thomas Aquinas.

units.titel: The third article: no lordship for the clergy
units.orig: Tercio, quod dominium seculare super diviciis et bonis temporalibus, quod contra preceptum Christi clerus occupat in preiudicium sui officii et dampnum brachii secularis, ab ipso auferatur et tollatur et ipse clerus ad regulam evangelicam et vitam apostolicam, qua Christus vixit cum suis apostolis, reducatur iuxta sentenciam salvatoris Mathie X° dicentis: et convocatis XII apostolis suis misit eos precipiens et dicens: nolite possidere aurum neque argentum neque pecuniam in zonis vestris. Et Mathie XX°: principes gencium dominantur eorum et, qui maiores sunt, potestatem exercent in eos; non ita erit inter vos. [...]
units.en: Third, that the secular lordship over riches and temporal goods which the clergy holds against the command of Christ, to the prejudice of its office and the damage of the secular arm, be taken and removed from it, and that the clergy itself be brought back to the rule of the gospel and the apostolic life which Christ lived with his apostles, according to the saying of the Saviour in Matthew 10, who, having called his twelve apostles, sent them out, commanding and saying: 'Possess neither gold nor silver nor money in your purses.' And Matthew 20: 'The princes of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them; it shall not be so among you.' [...]
units.note: The article that served the nobility best: in the following years lords and towns took much of the Church's land. It echoes Jerome's account of Hus before the council, the patrimony of the churches owed to the poor and squandered on pomp (Poggio [5]), and, further back, the Franciscan argument about apostolic poverty. The cut piles up proof-texts from both Testaments, the canons and St Bernard.

units.titel: The fourth article: public sins to be punished
units.orig: Quarto, quod omnia peccata mortalia et specialiter publica alieque deordinaciones legi dei contrarie in quolibet statu rite et racionabiliter per eos, ad quos spectat, prohibeantur et destruantur. Que qui agunt, digni sunt morte, non solum qui ea faciunt, sed qui consenciunt facientibus, ut sunt in populo fornicaciones, comessaciones, furta, homicidia, mendacia, periuria, artes superflue, dolose et supersticiose, questus avari, usure et cetera hiis similia. In clero autem sunt simoniace hereses et exacciones pecuniarum a baptismo, a confirmacione, a confessione, pro eukaristie sacramento, pro sacro oleo, a matrimonio [...], pro prebendis et beneficiis, pro prelaciis, dignitatibus, personatibus, palliis et empcionibus et vendicionibus indulgenciarum et alie innumere hereses, que ex hiis oriuntur et polluunt ecclesiam Christi [...].
units.en: Fourth, that all mortal sins, and especially public ones, and other disorders contrary to the law of God, in every estate, be forbidden and destroyed duly and reasonably by those whose office it is. Those who do such things are worthy of death, not only those who do them but those who consent to those who do them: such as, among the people, fornication, gluttony, theft, murder, lies, perjury, superfluous, deceitful and superstitious crafts, greedy gain, usury and the like. Among the clergy, the simoniac heresies and the exaction of money for baptism, for confirmation, for confession, for the sacrament of the Eucharist, for the holy oil, for marriage [...], for prebends and benefices, for prelacies, dignities, parsonages, palls, and the buying and selling of indulgences, and the countless other heresies that spring from these and pollute the Church of Christ [...].
units.note: The broadest article, and the most dangerous: it hands the punishment of public sin to 'those whose office it is', and the radicals could read that as a licence for themselves. The list of the clergy's charges begins with the sacraments and ends with indulgences, where Hus's open break with Rome had begun in 1412. 'Worthy of death' is Paul's phrase (Romans 1:32). The cuts shorten the list of fees and the closing exhortation.

sections.blurb: Sigismund crowned in the castle while Prague held out, the reliquaries melted for soldiers' pay, and the crusade leaving the field cursing its own commander.

units.titel: A king crowned in a castle
units.orig: Item XXVIII die Julii, dominico die scilicet post Jacobi, hora XII rex Sigismundus in castro Pragensi presentibus non omnibus baronibus nec scabinis Pragensibus in regem Boemie coronatur, facitque ibidem multos novos milites nullum penitus actum militarem prius pro communi bono ostendentes. Et sic a vulgo non veri, sed depicti milites sunt nuncupati. Item eodem die coronacionis sinistre et sequenti rex Sigismundus receptis ecclesie Pragensis et cenobii sancti Georgii capitibus, manibus, monstranciis, ceterisque de auro vel argento clenodiis concutere iubet et stipendia prebet promittens meliora facere, dum deus dederit regno pacem et quietem. Quorum igitur peccatum gravius, eorum scilicet, qui ligneas, aut eorum, qui argenteas ymagines destruxerunt? Item XXX die Julii, qui fuit tercius dies post regis coronacionem, totalis exercitus combustis tentoriis de campo recedit, regi Sigismundo velud hereticorum fautori et deceptori turpiter maledicentes.
units.en: Item, on the 28th day of July, that is the Sunday after St James, at the twelfth hour, King Sigismund was crowned king of Bohemia in Prague Castle, not all the barons being present, nor the aldermen of Prague; and there he made many new knights who had never shown any knightly deed for the common good. And so the people called them not true but painted knights. Item, on the same day of the ill-omened coronation and the next, King Sigismund took the heads, hands and monstrances and the other jewels of gold and silver of the church of Prague and of the convent of St George, had them broken up and paid his soldiers with them, promising to make better ones when God should give the kingdom peace and quiet. Whose sin, then, is the graver: theirs who destroyed images of wood, or his who destroyed images of silver? Item, on the 30th day of July, the third day after the king's coronation, the whole army burned its tents and left the field, cursing King Sigismund shamefully as a patron and deceiver of heretics.
units.note: Sigismund was crowned in St Vitus's cathedral inside the castle, which his garrison held, by Archbishop Conrad of Vechta, while the city below stood against him. The 'heads and hands' are the reliquaries of the cathedral and of St George's convent: the king who led a crusade against image-breakers melted down the saints to pay his army. On 2 September 1415 the lords had called him their heir and hoped him innocent (Protest [2]); in July 1420 the Praguers would not have him, and his own crusaders cursed him as a friend of heretics. He held the crown and not the kingdom: Bohemia accepted him only in 1436, a year before his death.
